expect.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
expect.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
expect.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
expect.baseFinding: The climbing starts DIRECTLY ABOVE THE GAP. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an OPEN BENCH, and above the bench you cross a SNOWFIELD into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's LEFT for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

expect.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
expect.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
expect.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

expect.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
expect.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout

The route is guarded by a RIDGE NOTCH, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a LARGE VERTICAL CRACK forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. value.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
value.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.
value.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford below the lake: cold and swift, and serious in snowmelt
Chief Creek ford near the head of Waptus Lake
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Very long approach far from help, with no cell coverage

expect.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
expect.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
expect.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
expect.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
expect.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

expect.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
expect.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
expect.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
expect.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
expect.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

value.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
value.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the Dutch Miller Gap trail climbs past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap, where the northeast face scramble starts. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
value.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
value.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
value.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

ops.expect: From the Trinity Trailhead, follow the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) about 1.5 miles past the Chiwawa River Trail junction (3,200 ft), then leave the trail and climb forested, brushy, and open slopes southwestward to King Lake (5,940 ft), which has good camping. From the lake, climb directly south to a notch on Buck's east ridge, cross to the south side of the ridge, contour around the next ESE ridge onto the low-angle southeast slopes, and bear WNW to the saddle between the south and middle summits before scrambling up rubbly, slabby schist to the middle (highest) or north summit. An alternative, longer approach reaches the peak's west/southwest slopes via Buck Creek Pass and High Pass.
ops.value: The usual way up comes from the west, which means a long way round even though the peak stands only about three miles from Trinity. From the Trinity Trailhead, the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) climbs about 9.6 miles and 3,100 ft to Buck Creek Pass. From the pass an unmaintained high route winds around the west side of Liberty Cap and south to High Pass; contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839, and walk down into Louis Creek Basin to camp. From the basin, broad pumice, talus and low-angle snow lead up the south and southwest slopes to the crest, and loose, slabby schist with one short Class 3-4 step near a horn goes to the summit. Some parties come in over Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley instead. A direct line from King Lake on the east side exists but is brushy, involves a river ford, and is seldom used.

ops.expect: Start at the Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Lake Trailhead (aka Esmeralda Trailhead, elev. ~4,300 ft) at the end of FR-9737, and take Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394. At about 0.4 mi you'll hit a signed junction with the Ingalls Way / Longs Pass Trail (#1390); stay straight/left to remain on the Esmeralda Basin Trail (the right fork climbs to Lake Ingalls and is off-limits to dogs). From here the trail follows an old mining road up the North Fork Teanaway drainage through subalpine forest, crossing a couple of small side-creeks (these are the last dependable water before the basin opens up — fill up here in late season). Around 2-3 mi the trail breaks out into the wildflower meadows of Esmeralda Basin proper, with the craggy Esmeralda Peaks visible directly ahead. From roughly 3 mi (~5,600-5,800 ft) the trail begins climbing via rockier switchbacks, skirting the north side of Ingalls Peak, and tops out at Fortune Creek Pass (~5,900-6,000 ft, ~3.5 mi from the TH) — a barren, open saddle with views toward Mt. Stuart, Hawkins Mountain, and (on a clear day) Rainier. Leave the maintained trail at or just below the pass and angle east/northeast off-trail onto the open talus and scree slopes on the south/southwest aspect of Esmeralda's west (true) summit. This last stretch is roughly 900-1,100 ft of unmaintained, sustained Class 2 talus/scree scrambling with some minor route-finding through boulder bands — parties note a rockier crux band partway up that's easiest skirted to the west, and a boulder-field alternative exists farther west if the direct scree gully is too loose. Watch for rockfall from parties above/below on this loose terrain, lingering snow patches in the gully into early summer (traction/axe useful then), and generally no water once you leave the basin meadows.
ops.value: Start at the De Roux trailhead and campground (~3,800 ft), on the left about 8 miles up gravel FR-9737 beyond the end of the paved North Fork Teanaway Road. Take the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 west, crossing the North Fork Teanaway and then De Roux Creek on bridges. About a mile in, keep right where the De Roux spur branches left, on the trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. The trail climbs steadily up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, crosses the creek again on rocks or logs (awkward in snowmelt), passes several waterfalls, and makes its last switchback across a talus ridge at roughly 5,500-5,600 ft, where a house-sized boulder sits beside the tread. Leave the trail there on the boulder's climber's left and head up the hillside on a northeast bearing. Above is about 1,100 ft of sustained Class 2 scree and talus with no marked path; the line beneath the southwest ridge and the talus farther to climber's right both go, and a boulder field farther west is an alternative if the direct slope is too loose. The top 100-150 ft is loose broken rock. The west summit is a walk-up and very slightly higher than the east summit, which is the one the maps mark; most parties tag both. The round trip is about 7 miles with roughly 3,100 ft of gain, and there is no water once you leave the valley trail.

ops.expect: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling. Retrace the ascent line: descend the same Class 2 talus/scree slope back down to Fortune Creek Pass, taking care on the loose scree (many parties find it faster and safer to plunge-step or glissade lingering snow in the gully in early season rather than fighting the talus). From the pass, drop back onto the maintained Esmeralda Basin Trail #1394 and follow it back down through the meadows and forest to the trailhead, retracing the ~3.5 mi hike-in. The two summits of Esmeralda Peaks are close enough that some parties traverse between the east and west high points along the connecting ridge before descending the same southwest gully — this adds minor Class 2-3 ridge scrambling but no additional technical gear. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are reported on this route; the only real descent hazards are loose rock underfoot and reduced visibility route-finding back to the correct gully in whiteout/low-cloud conditions given the broad, similar-looking talus slopes above Fortune Creek Pass.

ops.expect: From the Alpental day-use trailhead (~3,120 ft, at the end of Alpental Road via I-90 Exit 52), start on the Snow Lake Trail (#1013), a wide, well-graded trail that climbs through old avalanche-path brush and second-growth forest below the ski area's lower lift line. At roughly 1.8 miles and about 720 ft of gain, leave the main Snow Lake Trail where a boot path splits left (southwest) toward Source Lake rather than continuing right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water before the basin steepens, and worth treating and topping off here — then follow the use trail along the lake's north/east shore into the open basin beneath The Tooth and Chair Peak (Source Lake, ~3,400 ft). From the lake the tread becomes an intermittent boot-track over boulder-hop terrain and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south), staying beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant Peak's east side, and cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as "the Thumbtack" to reach the mouth of a steep scree-and-talus gully splitting Bryant's southeast face — this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the "Bryant Couloir"/"wonder gully," and it is an active avalanche path in winter and spring, so avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm. Ascend the gully favoring its far climber's-right side, which has noticeably firmer footing than the loose center and left. The gully tops out on the Bryant–Chair connecting ridge; from there work south over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. If the block still holds snow, the final scramble is easy Class 3 with little real exposure; in bare/dry conditions the only reasonable line is around the north (climber's left) side on exposed, distinctly loose Class 3 rock — test every hold. Overall this is about a 9.5-mile round trip with on the order of 3,000–3,400 ft of net gain to the 5,801 ft summit; plan 4–6 hours trailhead-to-summit for a fit party, more if the gully still holds snow requiring axe/crampons.
ops.value: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.

ops.expect: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble — there is no rappelling and no fixed anchors on the standard Southeast Slopes route; rappels = 0. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the same exposed, loose Class 3 stretch on the summit block's north side (or the easier snow-covered line if it's still in), then pick back across the ridge and talus to the head of the southeast gully. Stay on the ascent line — climber's right — on the way down; parties who drift climber's-left in this gully have gotten cliffed out above steep, loose dirt and been forced to down-scramble exposed, vegetated terrain to regain the route, so don't try to shortcut the fall line. Descend the gully facing in (plunge-stepping or using an axe if snow remains) through its steeper upper section, easing into a talus/boulder walk-down lower down. Because this gully doubles as a backcountry-ski descent and documented avalanche path, avoid it in the morning after a hard freeze-thaw cycle or following fresh snow loading in shoulder-season conditions. From the gully base, retrace the traverse beneath Bryant's cliffs back through Great Scott Basin to Source Lake, then rejoin the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) for the final descent to the Alpental trailhead. Note for context: a separate, considerably harder winter line up Bryant's northeast ridge has been descended with three 60m rappels (summit anchor to a ridge col/gendarme, a second 60m lowering past steep terrain, and a final rap down an ice step) — but that is a distinct technical route, not this standard Southeast Slopes scramble, and does not apply here.
ops.value: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappels and no fixed anchors. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully, facing in where it is steep, then return across the talus and down the ridge to Hemlock Pass, keeping to the ascent line around the cliff bands rather than cutting down the fall line. From the pass, follow the Denny Creek Trail back down to the trailhead. The steep gully between Bryant and Chair Peak on the Source Lake side is a separate line and an avalanche path in winter and spring; it is not a descent from this route.

expect.baseFinding:
THE THUMBTACK IS THE LANDMARK YOU WALK PAST, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONE IMMEDIATELY BEYOND IT. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

WHAT THE GULLY IS, IN OTHER WORDS: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

THE FOOTING TEST TELLS YOU WHERE TO BE WITHIN IT: climb favouring the FAR CLIMBERS' RIGHT side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

ops.expect: The South Route begins at the Dingford Creek Trailhead (also signed/known as the Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, ~1,550 ft), reached via I-90 Exit 34 and the rough, high-clearance/4WD-recommended Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) — the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead further up the road is no longer vehicle-accessible, so Dingford Creek is now the actual start. Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permits (free, required May 15–Oct 31) are at the trailhead register; there's a vault toilet but no potable water. From the trailhead, follow the Middle Fork Trail (#1003), which becomes the Dutch Miller Gap Trail (#1030), east up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley: a footbridge crossing of the Middle Fork at about 4.5 miles, then a steady, moderate climb to Hardscrabble Horse Camp (~7.7 mi) with open views of rockslides, waterfalls, and jagged peaks including Iron Cap itself across the valley (bikes and stock traffic are permitted only up to this point). Beyond Hardscrabble the trail crosses several avalanche-path openings and re-enters forest, reaching a steel bridge at Pedro Camp (~13 mi) and the Williams Lake Trail (#1031) junction at 14.2 mi (Williams Lake is a worthwhile water source/camp detour 1 mile off-route if backpacking in). The main trail continues through heather-and-huckleberry meadows to Dutch Miller Gap itself (~15.2 mi, ~5,000 ft), the low pass separating the Snoqualmie and Foss/Skykomish drainages. From the gap, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country north-northwest, contouring and ascending open talus, heather benches, and scree/dirt slopes on Iron Cap's south aspect toward the Iron Cap Lake basin, then up onto the west ridge for the final class 2–3 scramble to the 6,347 ft summit. This upper cross-country section is unmarked and route-finding is the crux of the approach — expect loose rock and dirt underfoot, occasional steep heather ('veggie') sections, and limited cairning; a map/GPS track is strongly advised since visibility-dependent cliff bands can cliff out a poorly chosen line. Water is reliable along the Middle Fork and at creek crossings/Williams Lake but scarce once you leave the valley floor above the gap, so tank up before the final push. Given the ~34-mile round trip and ~4,700–5,000 ft of cumulative gain, most parties treat this as a backpack (camping near Hardscrabble, Pedro Camp, or Williams Lake) rather than a single push, though strong parties have done it car-to-car. From the ridge, a short 3rd-class downclimb drops into a notch; beyond it a wide ramp traverses (no sidehilling) below the summit block to meet the broad north ridge, which leads via easy red-rock/dirt scrambling to the true summit.
ops.value: Start at the West Fork Foss River trailhead (~1,650 ft): from US 2 at Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68), then left on FR 6835 (signed for Trail 1064) for its last 1.9 miles to the trailhead. Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permits are at the trailhead. The West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 reaches Trout Lake at 1.6 miles, then climbs to Copper Lake (4.2 miles, about 2,400 ft of gain) and continues past Little Heart Lake to Big Heart Lake (7.3 miles, about 3,300 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From Big Heart, go cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake, to Chetwoot Lake, the usual camp. From Chetwoot, climb talus and heather toward Point 6077, pass it on the east through more talus, and gain Iron Cap's west ridge for easy Class 3 scrambling. A short third-class downclimb drops into a notch; beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, without sidehilling, to the broad north ridge, and easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the 6,347 ft summit. A variation climbs from the Iron Cap Lake outlet on ledges around the nose of the north ridge. Route-finding through the boulder fields is the crux of the approach: cairns are sparse, and a map or GPS track is strongly advised. Most parties take two to three days, about 24 miles round trip.

ops.expect: Descent reverses the ascent line: downclimb the loose red-tinged rock, dirt, and scree of the summit ridges back to the talus benches above Iron Cap Lake basin, then drop back down to Dutch Miller Gap and rejoin the maintained Dutch Miller Gap/Middle Fork Trail (#1030/#1003) for the long walk out to the Dingford Creek Trailhead. This is a class 2–3 scramble route with no fixed anchors or rappel stations — it is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent. The main hazards on the way down are the same loose, dirt-over-rock terrain that makes the ascent's crux (test holds carefully, especially when wet or in the early season with residual snow patches), plus the route-finding challenge of picking the correct gully/ledge system back down to the basin rather than getting cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands — parties in this area have reported wandering into steep 'veggie' terrain when they lost the correct line, so retracing your ascent track (or using a GPS track) is the most reliable way down. Once back at Dutch Miller Gap, it's a straightforward, well-graded trail walk of roughly 15 miles back to the trailhead with the elevation loss front-loaded near the gap and gentler grades through the lower valley.
ops.value: Descent reverses the ascent or loops through the Iron Cap Lake basin. From the summit, follow the broad north ridge down on easy red-tinged rock and dirt, then either return across the ramp and up out of the notch onto the west ridge and down the talus to Chetwoot Lake, or continue down the north ridge to Iron Cap Lake and work back to camp through the lake basin. This is a Class 2-3 walk-off with no fixed anchors or rappels. The main hazards are loose dirt over rock, especially when wet or with snow patches early in the season, and picking the wrong line: parties who lose the ramp or wander east end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands or in steep heather, so retrace your ascent track. From Chetwoot, reverse the cross-country leg over Atrium Ridge to Big Heart Lake and walk the West Fork Foss trail about 7.3 miles back to the trailhead.

expect.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
expect.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
expect.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
expect.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
expect.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

expect.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
expect.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
expect.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
expect.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
expect.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

value.name: Chetwoot Lake
value.notes: The base for the climb: reached off-trail from Big Heart Lake over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake. Much quieter than Big Heart. The climb to Iron Cap's west ridge starts from here.
